raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old man living in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and working as a marble and tile setter in the construction industry, was admitted to the hospital with acute, diffuse abdominal pain, arterial hypotension, and jaundice. The patient reported exposure to floodwater and ingestion of contaminated water 10 days prior to symptom onset. On admission, an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed pneumoperitoneum near the gallbladder and bile ducts. An exploratory laparotomy with cholecystectomy was performed, but no gastroduodenal perforation was observed. The patient remained in the intensive care unit (ICU), where he developed jaundice, acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis, and alveolar hemorrhage necessitating orotracheal intubation. Laboratory investigation confirmed leptospirosis by two consecutive serological tests: ELISA-IgM and a microscopic agglutination test for the serovar Cynopteri, with a titer of 1/800. He was treated with ceftriaxone for 14 days, leading to clinical and laboratory improvement.
After two weeks hospitalized, the patient experienced multiple episodes of severe enterorrhagia and required a massive transfusion of 10 units of red blood cells. Due to ongoing bleeding, a total colectomy with terminal ileostomy was performed, and the resected samples were sent for histopathological examination. The patient showed clinical improvement and was discharged for outpatient follow-up.
One month later, he returned to the hospital with a surgical wound infection. An abdominal CT scan showed diffuse parietal thickening of the small bowel loops, mild distension without obstructive factors, and diffuse densification of the peritoneal layers (Figure 1A). At this time, histopathology from the first surgery revealed a necrotizing granulomatous inflammatory process, a transmural ulcer with hyphae suggestive of mucormycosis (Figure 1B), fibrino-leukocytic peritonitis, acute purulent periappendicitis, reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, and chronic epiploitis with suppuration foci. Mucormycosis was subsequently confirmed by PCR on the paraffin-embedded tissue sample from the total colectomy (Figure 1C). The patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B at a 5 mg/kg/day dosage for 7 weeks, followed by oral posaconazole suspension at 400 mg twice per day. Follow-up abdominal CT scans showed complete clinical and radiological resolution after five months of posaconazole therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male construction worker presented with acute diffuse abdominal pain, arterial hypotension, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the hospital in São Paulo, Brazil, with acute diffuse abdominal pain, hypotension, and jaundice beginning 10 days after exposure to floodwaters and ingestion of contaminated water.
subjective.past_medical_history: Worked as a marble and tile setter in the construction industry in São Paulo, Brazil; exposed to floodwater and ingested contaminated water 10 days before symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for diffuse abdominal pain and jaundice; hospital course later complicated by massive enterorrhagia and surgical wound infection.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with arterial hypotension, jaundice, and acute diffuse abdominal pain.
objective.routine_investigations: Demonstrated hyperbilirubinemia and acute renal failure during ICU admission.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission abdominal CT showed pneumoperitoneum adjacent to the gallbladder and bile ducts. Exploratory laparotomy with cholecystectomy found no gastroduodenal perforation. After severe enterorrhagia at 2 weeks, total colectomy with terminal ileostomy was performed; histopathology of surgical specimens revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, transmural ulceration with broad hyphae suggestive of mucormycosis, fibrino-leukocytic peritonitis, acute purulent periappendicitis, reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, and chronic suppurative epiploitis. Tissue PCR on paraffin-embedded colectomy tissue confirmed mucormycosis. Readmission abdominal CT at 1 month showed diffuse small bowel wall thickening, mild non-obstructive distension, and peritoneal layer densification.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed severe leptospirosis (Weil's syndrome with jaundice, acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis, and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage requiring intubation) complicated by gastrointestinal mucormycosis. Leptospirosis was confirmed by two consecutive positive serological assays: Leptospira IgM ELISA and microscopic agglutination test (MAT) positive for serovar Cynopteri at 1:800 titer. Treated with IV ceftriaxone for 14 days, hemodialysis, and mechanical ventilation. Complicated after 2 weeks by massive enterorrhagia requiring 10 units of packed red blood cells and total colectomy with terminal ileostomy. Upon histopathological and tissue PCR confirmation of intestinal mucormycosis 1 month later, he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day for 7 weeks) followed by oral posaconazole suspension (400 mg twice daily for 5 months), achieving complete clinical and radiological resolution.
